Long-term stewardship is held by the DOE Office of Legacy Management.

claims.text: THE DOCUMENTED FEDERAL HOLE IN THE GROUND NEXT TO DULCE, TWELVE YEARS BEFORE THE RUMOUR. On 10 December 1967 the US Atomic Energy Commission detonated a 29-kiloton-yield nuclear device in the emplacement well GB-E at a depth of 4,227 feet, twelve miles southwest of Dulce in the Carson National Forest, on a 640-acre site now managed by the DOE Office of Legacy Management. This is a record of Project Gasbuggy. It is adjacency and precedence, and it is NOT a claim that Gasbuggy caused the rumour.

claims.text: Project Gasbuggy, the first natural-gas reservoir stimulation experiment of the Plowshare programme, left a 640-acre site in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico under federal stewardship from the 1967 detonation through decommissioning in 1978, soil sampling in 1978, 1986, 2000 and 2002, and final surface remediation completed in September 2004. Liquid radioactive waste remains injected in the former cavity and a brass plaque on a concrete base marks the site.

claims.text: On 10 December 1967 the US Atomic Energy Commission detonated a 29-kiloton-yield nuclear device in the emplacement well GB-E at a depth of 4,227 feet, in an attempt to stimulate production of natural gas from the overlying gas-bearing Pictured Cliffs Formation. The site is 12 miles southwest of Dulce, New Mexico, in the Carson National Forest, totalling 640 acres.

claims.sourceText: DOE Office of Legacy Management Gasbuggy fact sheet, https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/GasbuggyFactSheet.pdf , read in full 2026-09-19
claims.text: THE FORTY-YEAR FEDERAL RETURN TO THE GROUND. AEC decommissioned and demobilised the site in 1978, injecting liquid radioactive waste into the former cavity and transporting solid radioactive waste to the Nevada Test Site. Soil sampling followed in 1978, 1986, 2000 and 2002; final surface remediation removed 5,562 cubic yards of contaminated soil and was completed in September 2004. A permanent monument, a brass plaque in a concrete base, was placed at the site.

claims.sourceText: DOE Office of Legacy Management Gasbuggy fact sheet, https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/GasbuggyFactSheet.pdf , read in full 2026-09-19
claims.text: Production testing through a reentry well, GB-ER, ran from July 1968 to October 1969 across five tests, producing 213 million cubic feet of natural gas that retained measurable radioactive constituents and had a significantly lower heat value than expected. In 1976 it was decided that no further testing would be conducted.

claims.sourceText: DOE Office of Legacy Management Gasbuggy fact sheet, https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/GasbuggyFactSheet.pdf , read in full 2026-09-19
claims.text: The detonation created a cavity and, as the overlying fractured rock collapsed into it, a rubble-filled collapse chimney. This was the first natural gas reservoir stimulation experiment in the Plowshare Program, jointly sponsored by the AEC, the US Department of the Interior and the El Paso Natural Gas Company.

claims.text: The DOE Office of Legacy Management holds long-term stewardship of the Gasbuggy site in Rio Arriba County, New Mexico, 640 acres in the Carson National Forest twelve miles southwest of Dulce, where the AEC detonated a 29-kiloton device at 4,227 feet on 10 December 1967. Liquid radioactive waste was injected into the former cavity on decommissioning in 1978 and final surface remediation removing 5,562 cubic yards of contaminated soil was completed in September 2004.
